newsitem.title: USA: Defunct drug prevents heart arteries re-clogging.
newsitem.headline: Defunct drug prevents heart arteries re-clogging.

text.p: A drug taken off the U.S. market because tests showed it reduced "good" cholesterol as well as "bad" may turn out to be a boon for angioplasty patients.

A team of Montreal doctors reported in Thursday's New England Journal of Medicine that the drug probucol can prevent heart arteries opened up by angioplasty from clogging up again, reducing the need for repeat surgery by 58 percent.
Angioplasty is a non-surgical procedure used to re-open clogged arteries by inflating a tiny balloon inserted into an artery by catheter.

The study of 317 volunteers, led by Dr. Jean-Claude Tardif of the Montreal Heart Institute, sought to tackle the frequent problem of arteries clogging up again, forcing patients to repeat the procedure or have bypass surgery.
Previous research had suggested that chemicals known as antioxidants may help keep the arteries open.

Tardif and his colleagues divided 317 patients into four groups, one of which got high doses of the antioxidant supplements beta carotene, vitamin C and vitamin E. Another got probucol, which is a powerful antioxidant. A third group received both treatments, while the fourth received placebos.
The treatments began four weeks before an angioplasty and continued for six months after the procedure. The arteries of those receiving probucol had the least amount of re-clogging.

Probucol, sold under the brand name Lorelco and manufactured by Hoechst Marion Roussel, a subsidairy of Hoechst AG, is no longer marketed in the United States, in part because it reduced both "good" and "bad" cholesterol and a Swedish study hinted that it might have other serious side effects, said Libby and Ganz. The drug remains available elsewhere.

A drop in "good" cholesterol was also seen in the new study, along with a tendency for diarrhoea to develop in 16 percent of the people who took the drug and 33 percent who took both the drug and the vitamins. Diarrhoea was reported in only two percent of the placebo recipients.
About 400,000 people undergo angioplasty in the United States each year, according to the American Heart Association.
